soru.x: The first option is correct: the topic is clear (weekday bread sales), it is measurable (10 percent), reasonable and time-bound (30 September). The others lack a number or a date. For example, “much more than our competitors” sounds bold, but it is neither measurable nor time-bound.

adimlar.baslik: MBO: setting objectives together with the employee
adimlar.anlatim:
It is easy to set objectives at the top and send them down, but then the employee does not own them. MBO (Management by Objectives) solves this problem. This systematic approach, introduced by Drucker in 1954, aligns the objectives of subordinates with the overall goals of the organization. The crucial part is this: employees take part in setting their own objectives and timelines.

Think of the logic in two parts. The first is alignment: each employee's objective is tied to a higher goal, so everyone's work adds to the company's direction. The second is participation: people commit more to an objective they set themselves. In a scenario, if a manager and an employee set personal objectives with deadlines together, and these support the department's goals, say MBO.

Watch out for a name trap: management by exception in Chapter 4 and MBO are completely different. Management by exception means the transactional leader steps in only for exceptions, that is, problems. MBO means setting objectives together.
adimlar.ornek: In a fictional language school, the head Sena shares the school's goal “to raise student satisfaction” with the teachers. Each teacher sits down with her and proposes a personal objective: one says “add two speaking clubs to every class by the end of March”, another says “bring homework feedback down to 48 hours by the end of term”. The objectives are tied to the overall goal and the employees took part in setting them: MBO.

soru.q: At a fictional software firm, each developer proposes personal quarterly targets with deadlines, and the manager links them to the department's goals. Which approach is this?
soru.x: The correct answer is Management by Objectives: employees take part in setting their objectives and timelines, and these are aligned with the organization's goals. Management by exception is tempting because the name is similar, but that is a transactional leadership method that steps in only for problems.

adimlar.baslik: Balanced Scorecard and KPI
adimlar.anlatim:
You cannot tell whether a company is doing well by looking only at profit: profit may be good today, while customers are leaving or employees are not growing at all. The Balanced Scorecard is the tool of Kaplan and Norton. It turns the mission, vision and strategy into specific, measurable goals and tracks them in four areas.

Financial: are we making money for our owners? Customer: are customers satisfied and loyal? Internal business processes: are our operations efficient and of high quality? Learning & growth: are our employees and the organization growing? This is where the word “balanced” in the name comes from: financial and non-financial measures are balanced. Also, leading measures (which signal the result in advance) and lagging measures (which show the result afterwards) are used together.

A KPI (key performance indicator) is a measurable value that shows how effectively a company is reaching its key business objectives. Do not mix up the two: a KPI is one measurable value, while the Balanced Scorecard is a whole framework that turns strategy into measurable goals in four areas. Exam trap: the Balanced Scorecard is not “only financial goals”.
adimlar.ornek: A fictional chain of bike repair shops tracks four areas: monthly profit (financial), the share of returning customers (customer), the average time of a repair (internal business processes) and the number of technicians who earn a certificate (learning & growth). “The share of returning customers is 60 percent” is one KPI on its own. The four areas together are the Balanced Scorecard.

soru.q: A hospital tracks the share of its staff who completed new training courses this year. In which Balanced Scorecard perspective does this measure belong?
soru.x: The correct answer is learning & growth: the question of this area is “are our employees and the organization growing?”. Internal business processes is tempting because training affects operations. But that perspective measures the efficiency and quality of operations, not the growth of people.

adimlar.baslik: CSR and the triple bottom line
adimlar.anlatim:
Should a company's success be measured only by its own profit? CSR (corporate social responsibility) means that companies manage their business processes in a way that produces an overall positive impact on society. Be careful: the definition does not talk about giving donations. It talks about the business processes themselves. The responsibility is inside the way the work is done.

The hard part of CSR is measuring it. Here the book links to the Balanced Scorecard: according to Crawford and Scaletta, the Balanced Scorecard can help to make CSR values measurable. So you can turn CSR into concrete goals that can be tracked too.

The triple bottom line means measuring performance in three dimensions: social, environmental and economic. In short, people, planet, profit. The logic of the name is this: the classic “bottom line” is profit, and this approach puts two more dimensions next to it. The examples in the slides are the Dow Jones Sustainability Index (DJSI), the UN's Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) for 2030 and Net Zero targets.

Keep the difference in mind: CSR is a management approach, while the triple bottom line is a way of measuring performance.
adimlar.ornek: A fictional chocolate maker publishes three tables in its annual report: the fair price paid to cocoa farmers and employee health (people), the factory's carbon emissions and water use (planet) and net profit (profit). It reports performance in three dimensions: the triple bottom line. Organizing its supply process so that it does not harm the farmers is CSR.

soru.q: A fictional ferry company publishes yearly results on passenger and crew well-being, fuel emissions and profit. Which concept does this reporting reflect?
soru.x: The correct answer is the triple bottom line: performance is measured in the social, environmental and economic dimensions, that is, people, planet and profit. The Balanced Scorecard is tempting because it also uses non-financial measures. But its four areas are financial, customer, internal processes, and learning and growth.

tuzaklar.yanlis: “An outcome statement that says what the organization wants to accomplish” is an objective.
tuzaklar.dogru: This is a goal. An objective is a precise, time-based and measurable action.

tuzaklar.yanlis: The Balanced Scorecard tracks only financial goals.
tuzaklar.dogru: It turns the mission and strategy into measurable goals and tracks them in four areas: financial, customer, internal processes, and learning and growth.

tuzaklar.yanlis: MBO and management by exception are the same approach.
tuzaklar.dogru: MBO means setting objectives together with the employee. Management by exception is transactional leadership that steps in only for problems.

tuzaklar.yanlis: A KPI and the Balanced Scorecard are the same thing.
tuzaklar.dogru: A KPI is one measurable value. The Balanced Scorecard is a whole framework with four perspectives.

tuzaklar.yanlis: The three dimensions of the triple bottom line are customer, employee and profit.
tuzaklar.dogru: The three dimensions are social, environmental and economic: people, planet, profit.

ozet: The planning chain: vision and mission, strategy, then goals and objectives.
A goal is an outcome statement that says what you want to accomplish. An objective is a precise, time-based and measurable action.
Time horizons: long term is 3 years or more, mid-range is 1 to 3 years, short term is less than 1 year.
SMART: an objective that is specific, measurable, achievable, realistic and time-bound.
MBO (Drucker, 1954): aligning individual objectives with the organization's goals, with employees taking part.
Balanced Scorecard (Kaplan and Norton): the financial, customer, internal processes, and learning and growth areas.
A KPI is a measurable value that shows how effectively key objectives are being reached.
CSR means managing processes in a way that has a positive impact on society. The Balanced Scorecard can make it measurable.
Triple bottom line: people, planet, profit.
lessons.aklinda: A goal is the place you are going, an objective is a measured step on the way there. The four questions of the scorecard: Money? Customers? Processes? Growth?
lessons.sinavda: In Part 1 this lesson mostly comes as definition questions: the definition of goal and objective, what the Balanced Scorecard does and its four areas, the letters of SMART, who introduced MBO. Sometimes you are also asked to find a SMART objective or a triple bottom line report among the options.

lessons.neden: Two people work for the same pay. Why does one throw themselves into the job while the other settles for the least effort? Motivation theories explain this. Part 1 asks about order, lists and classification here: Maslow's order, Herzberg's two lists, how ERG differs from Maslow, the referent in equity theory. If you learn the theories with their logic, the lists fall into place by themselves.
hedefler: Explain the definition of motivation and the performance equation.
Compare Maslow, ERG, Herzberg and McClelland as need-based theories.
Following Herzberg, place factors around the job and inside the job in the right group in a scenario.
Apply the four process theories (equity, expectancy, goal-setting, reinforcement) to an employee's behaviour.
Show the difference between distributive, procedural and interactional justice with an example.

adimlar.baslik: What motivation is and what decides performance
adimlar.anlatim:
Motivation, in the book's definition, is “the intention of achieving a goal, leading to goal-directed behaviour”. The definition has two parts: the intention inside and the goal-directed behaviour that can be seen from outside. Only wanting something does not count as motivation. That wish needs to turn into behaviour.

Motivation alone does not bring performance. The equation in the book: Performance = Motivation × Ability × Environment. The multiplication sign matters: if one of the three factors is zero, the result drops to zero too. A person who is very keen but does not know the job cannot perform well. A person who is skilled and keen but works with broken equipment cannot either. So a manager who sees low performance should look at all three factors and not say “there is no motivation” straight away.

The theories split into two families. Need-based theories ask what moves people: Maslow, ERG, Herzberg, McClelland. Process-based theories ask how motivation works: equity, expectancy, goal-setting, reinforcement. The exam asks which theory belongs to which family.
adimlar.ornek: In a fictional pastry shop, the apprentice Mert is very keen (motivation is high) and has finished a pastry course (ability is high), but the oven keeps breaking down (environment is weak). The cakes still burn. The master does not try to motivate him more. He has the oven repaired, and performance rises at once.

soru.q: A highly motivated and skilled nurse keeps making errors because the ward's equipment is outdated. According to the performance equation, which factor is holding her performance back?
soru.x: The correct answer is environment: the nurse is both keen and skilled, and the problem is in the place where she works. Motivation is tempting, because low performance is often blamed on it. But the equation has three factors, and the missing one here is the environment.

adimlar.baslik: Maslow: the hierarchy of needs
adimlar.anlatim:
Maslow orders human needs as a hierarchy with five levels, starting from the bottom: physiological (food, water, sleep), safety (being safe, and stability), social (relationships, friendship, belonging to a group), esteem (respect, status, recognition) and self-actualization (reaching your full potential). The name of this structure is Maslow's hierarchy.

The logic of the order is this: when you are hungry you do not care about friendship, and when you are not safe you do not care about status. When a lower need is met, the one above it comes forward. The key sentence in the book: a satisfied need no longer motivates. So you cannot motivate a person whose pay and job security are in place by offering more security. What moves them now is recognition or a chance to grow.

The way to remember the order is to climb from the most basic to the most abstract: first the body, then safety, then people, then respect, and last being yourself.
adimlar.ornek: In a fictional company, the warehouse worker Kaan cares only about overtime in the period when he can hardly pay his rent. When he moves to a permanent contract and gains security, he starts to eat lunch with the team and joins the company football team (social). A year later, what excites him most is being chosen “employee of the month” (esteem). Each need that is met stops motivating.

soru.q: An employee has a secure job, good friends at work and is respected by her whole team. According to Maslow, which need is most likely to motivate her now?
soru.x: The correct answer is self-actualization: the safety, social and esteem needs are met. A satisfied need no longer motivates, so the top level is next. Esteem is tempting, because recognition still feels nice. But in the scenario she has already won the respect of her team.

adimlar.baslik: ERG theory: three groups and stepping back
adimlar.anlatim:
Alderfer's ERG theory brings Maslow's five levels down to three groups. Existence is the basic material and physical needs, the sum of physiological and safety in Maslow. Relatedness is relationships with others, social in Maslow. Growth is personal development, esteem and self-actualization in Maslow.

The real difference is not in the number of groups. It is in the rules. First, there is no fixed order. Second, more than one need can be active at the same time. Third, and asked most often: frustration-regression. If a higher need is blocked, the person goes back to a lower need and puts more weight on it. In Maslow you only go up. In ERG you can go down when you are blocked.

Scenario clue: if someone cannot find a chance to grow and so turns to socializing or to asking for more money, this is the frustration-regression principle of ERG. Maslow cannot explain this behaviour, because his model has no going back.
adimlar.ornek: In a fictional advertising agency, the graphic designer Pinar has waited years for a promotion, but she is given no new responsibility (growth is blocked). After a while she stops talking about her career and puts all her energy into friendships and social events at the office (relatedness). Going back to the lower need when the higher one is blocked: frustration-regression.

soru.q: A lab technician who cannot get any training or promotion starts demanding much higher pay instead. Which idea explains this best?
soru.x: The correct answer is frustration-regression: when the growth need is blocked, the person puts more weight on the lower existence need, that is, money. Maslow is tempting, but in his hierarchy you only go up. ERG is the one that explains being blocked and going back.

adimlar.baslik: Herzberg's two factors and McClelland
adimlar.anlatim:
According to Herzberg, satisfaction and dissatisfaction at work are caused by different factors. That is why the theory is called the two-factor theory.

Hygiene factors are about the context of the job: company policies, supervision, working conditions, salary, safety and security. When they are missing they create dissatisfaction. When they are fixed they prevent dissatisfaction, but they do not motivate. The logic of the name: hygiene prevents illness, but it does not make you strong. Motivators are about the job itself: achievement, recognition, interesting work, responsibility, advancement and growth. These are what create real motivation.

The test for telling them apart: is this factor around the job or inside the job? Office temperature, job security and clear policies are around it, so they are hygiene. Full responsibility for a project is inside the job, so it is a motivator. The difference from Maslow: Maslow explains general human needs, Herzberg explains the source of satisfaction and dissatisfaction at work.

The fourth member of the need family is McClelland: three acquired needs, achievement, affiliation and power.
adimlar.ornek: In a fictional call centre, management replaces the air conditioners and brings salaries up to the market level. Complaints fall, but nobody works with more enthusiasm, because these are hygiene factors. Then each team is given responsibility for managing a whole customer group, and monthly recognition for achievement. Employees start to come up with ideas, because these are motivators.

soru.q: A factory manager wants to truly motivate her staff, not just reduce complaints. According to Herzberg, which action should she choose?
o: Let workers lead the redesign of a product line
Raise salaries to the industry average level
Install better heating in the production hall
Make the company leave policy clearer for all
soru.x: The first option is correct: leading the redesign of a product line offers responsibility and achievement, so it is a motivator. Raising salaries is tempting, but salary is a hygiene factor: it prevents dissatisfaction and does not create motivation.

adimlar.baslik: Equity theory and the three types of justice
adimlar.anlatim:
The first of the process theories is about fairness. Adams's equity theory says that people compare their own inputs (effort, loyalty, skill) and outcomes (pay, rewards) with a referent. The referent is the person or group you compare yourself with: a colleague who does the same job, or a friend at another company. What matters is not the absolute pay but the ratio: is your ratio of inputs to outcomes in balance with theirs?

Imbalance creates tension, and the person chooses one of five ways to reduce this tension: they lower their own input (work less), they ask for more, they distort their perceptions (they convince themselves that “the other one really works harder”), they change their referent, or they leave the job.

Justice is not only about equity. Distributive justice means the outcomes are fair, procedural justice means the process is fair, and interactional justice means respectful treatment. Even if a pay rise is shared out correctly, procedural justice is damaged if the decision was made through a secret and arbitrary process.
adimlar.ornek: In a fictional restaurant, the waiter Derya learns that she gets the same share of tips as Umut, who is new and serves fewer tables. Umut is her referent. Derya finds the ratio unfair and stops taking extra tables: she restores the balance by lowering her input, equity theory.

soru.q: Two team leaders receive the same bonus, which seems fair. Then one learns the bonus rules were decided in secret and changed without explanation. Which type of justice is harmed?
soru.x: The correct answer is procedural justice: the outcome looks fair, but the decision process is secret and arbitrary. Distributive justice is tempting, but that is about whether the outcome that is shared out, the bonus, is fair. Here the problem is in the process, not in the outcome.

adimlar.baslik: Expectancy theory: the chain of effort, performance and reward
adimlar.anlatim:
Expectancy theory sees motivation as a chain: people work harder when they believe that effort will lead to performance, and that performance will lead to rewards they value. The chain has three links.

Expectancy: the belief that effort will lead to the desired performance. “If I work hard, can I hit this target?” Instrumentality: the belief that performance will lead to the reward. “If I hit it, will I really get the reward?” Valence: how valuable the reward is for the person. “Does this reward matter to me?”

The logic: if one of the links breaks, the chain does not work. A person who believes the target is impossible does not push (low expectancy). A person who thinks the reward will not be given, even if they hit the target, does not push (low instrumentality). If the reward means nothing to them, again they do not push (low valence). In a scenario, find which link is broken: “I can't do it” is expectancy, “they won't give it” is instrumentality, “I don't want it” is valence.
adimlar.ornek: A fictional bookshop chain promises a weekend holiday to any employee who sells 500 books in a month. The new employee Melis thinks her shop is small and that she will never reach this number, so she does not push at all. The reward is attractive and she believes it will be given, but she does not believe that effort will lead to performance: low expectancy.

soru.q: A courier believes he could easily hit the delivery target, but he knows past bonuses were never actually paid. In expectancy theory, which link is weak?
soru.x: The correct answer is instrumentality: the courier believes he can hit the target, but he does not believe that performance will lead to the reward. Expectancy is tempting, but that is the belief that effort will lead to performance, and the courier is already sure about that.

adimlar.baslik: Goal-setting theory: the power of a goal and its price
adimlar.anlatim:
Locke and Latham's goal-setting theory says that specific and challenging goals, that is, SMART goals, raise performance. According to the book, the theory is supported by more than 1,000 studies. SMART, which you learned in c7a, turns into a motivation tool here.

Why does it work? SMART goals do four things: they give direction (you know what to focus on), they give energy, they challenge you (difficulty pushes people to make an effort) and they force creative thinking (you look for new ways to reach the goal). Saying “do your best” does none of these.

The book also lists three downsides of the theory. Tunnel vision: locking onto the goal and not seeing what is around it. Neglecting work that is not measured: if the goal is the number of sales, work that is not measured, such as helping the customer, is forgotten. Unethical behaviour: breaking rules to hit the goal. The exam likes these downsides.

Do not mix it up with expectancy: goal-setting looks at how the goal itself is built, while expectancy looks at the chain of beliefs between effort, performance and reward.
adimlar.ornek: A fictional call centre gives its agents the goal “close 80 calls a day”. Because the goal is clear and challenging, performance rises (goal-setting theory). But some agents start to hang up on difficult customers without solving their problem, and nobody updates the training notes: neglect of work that is not measured, and unethical behaviour.

soru.q: A fictional sales team is given a tough monthly target. Sales rise, but staff stop helping customers with returns, which nobody measures. Which downside of goal setting is this?
o: Ignoring work that is not measured
Lower energy because goals are vague
soru.x: The first option is correct: the team focuses on sales, which are measured, and drops help with returns, which is not measured. The second option may look tempting, but here the goal is not vague. On the contrary, it is clear and challenging. The problem is the neglect of work that falls outside the goal.

adimlar.baslik: Reinforcement theory: the consequences of behaviour
adimlar.anlatim:
Reinforcement theory is the simplest process theory: behaviour is shaped by the consequences that follow it. The book lists four tools and splits them into two groups by their effect.

Those that increase behaviour: positive reinforcement and negative reinforcement. Those that decrease behaviour: extinction and punishment. The example of positive reinforcement is simple: praising an employee who hands in reports on time makes them repeat that behaviour. So is the example of punishment: giving a written warning to an employee who comes late aims to reduce lateness.

The biggest trap is in the name. The word “negative” may make you think of punishment, but in the book negative reinforcement is in the group that increases behaviour. The word “reinforcement” in its name tells you this. Punishment is in the group that decreases. Extinction is in the decreasing group too: the name means “dying out”, so the behaviour fades over time. In the exam, the answer to “which ones increase behaviour?” is the two reinforcements.

The difference from the other process theories: equity, expectancy and goal-setting look at the comparison, the belief and the goal inside a person's head. Reinforcement looks at the consequences of behaviour that come from outside.
adimlar.ornek: In a fictional football academy, the coach praises the children who come early to training in front of everyone, every time, and the number who come early grows: positive reinforcement. A player who keeps distracting others in training is left on the bench for one match. This is a punishment that aims to reduce the behaviour.

soru.q: A trainer wants to increase a desired behaviour in her team. According to reinforcement theory as presented in the book, which pair of tools both increase behaviour?
soru.x: The correct answer is positive and negative reinforcement: both increase behaviour. Negative reinforcement and punishment is tempting, because the word “negative” sounds like punishment. But punishment and extinction are in the group that decreases behaviour.

tuzaklar.yanlis: Fixing the office temperature, job security and clear policies motivate the employee.
tuzaklar.dogru: These are hygiene factors: they prevent dissatisfaction and do not motivate. Factors inside the job, such as full responsibility for a project, are motivators.

tuzaklar.yanlis: An employee who lowers their effort after seeing a colleague get the same reward for less effort is explained by Maslow.
tuzaklar.dogru: This is equity theory: the employee compares the ratio of inputs to outcomes with a referent and restores the balance by lowering their input.

tuzaklar.yanlis: ERG is a three-level version of Maslow, and its rules are the same.
tuzaklar.dogru: In ERG there is no fixed order, more than one need can be active at the same time, and you can go back through frustration-regression.

tuzaklar.yanlis: Maslow and Herzberg answer the same question.
tuzaklar.dogru: Maslow explains general human needs. Herzberg explains the source of satisfaction and dissatisfaction at work.

tuzaklar.yanlis: Negative reinforcement is a type of punishment and decreases behaviour.
tuzaklar.dogru: In the book, negative reinforcement is in the group that increases behaviour. The ones that decrease it are extinction and punishment.

tuzaklar.yanlis: Equity theory is a need theory.
tuzaklar.dogru: Maslow, ERG, Herzberg and McClelland are need-based. Equity, expectancy, goal-setting and reinforcement are process-based.

ozet: Motivation is the intention that leads to goal-directed behaviour. Performance is motivation times ability times environment.
Maslow's order: physiological, safety, social, esteem, self-actualization. A satisfied need does not motivate.
ERG: existence, relatedness, growth. No fixed order, more than one need at the same time, going back when blocked.
Herzberg: hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction, motivators truly motivate.
McClelland's three acquired needs: achievement, affiliation and power.
Equity: we compare our ratio of inputs to outcomes with a referent. The types of justice are distributive, procedural and interactional.
Expectancy: expectancy, instrumentality and valence. If one link of the chain breaks, motivation falls.
Goal-setting: SMART goals give direction, energy and challenge. They carry the risk of tunnel vision and unethical behaviour.
Reinforcement: the two reinforcements increase behaviour, extinction and punishment decrease it.
lessons.aklinda: Maslow's ladder: Food, Safety, Friends, Fame, Fulfilment. Herzberg: around the job is hygiene, inside the job is a motivator.
lessons.sinavda: In Part 1 this lesson mostly comes as order, list and matching questions: Maslow's order from the bottom up, which factor is hygiene and which is a motivator, how ERG differs from Maslow, what a referent is, and which theory is need-based and which is process-based. In short scenarios you are asked to link the behaviour to the right theory.
